memos.headline: XOM and CAT Lead While MSFT and UNH Collapse — Bifurcated Tape Demands Selectivity
memos.body: I see a deeply split market as of 2026-03-27. XOM is at its 52-week high with RSI 76.1 and +49% relative strength vs SPY over 12 weeks — a parabolic move that demands respect but also caution on chasing. CAT is the second-strongest name, +28% relative strength over 12 weeks, sitting near its 50-day mean with a neutral RSI of 46 — the cleanest long setup in the universe. On the other side, MSFT at RSI 22.3 and -34.2% from its 52-week high is in freefall with no sign of stabilization; I would not try to catch that knife until it reclaims its 50-day mean (~$410). UNH is even worse structurally, down 56.8% from its high with persistent negative relative strength, and I see no technical reason to step in. GOOGL's RSI of 25.1 after a -8.9% week is deeply oversold and could bounce, but the 4-week relative weakness of -4.4% vs SPY tells me this is not yet a high-conviction entry.

views.note: At 52-week highs with dominant relative strength (+49% vs SPY over 12w); would trim if RSI breaks below 60 or price loses 155.
Strong 12w and 26w uptrend (+28% rel strength), healthy RSI 46 pullback near 50d mean — best risk/reward setup; invalidated below 650.
RSI 22.3, -34% drawdown, -25.5% below 200d mean, and -19% relative weakness over 12w — textbook downtrend with no base; need a weekly close above 410 to reconsider.

memos.headline: NVDA and MSFT Lead on Earnings Power; UNH's Near-Zero Margin Is a Red Flag
memos.body: I see the clearest durable earnings power in NVDA and MSFT. NVDA posted Q4 revenue of $68.1B (+73.2% YoY) with a 63.1% net margin and only $8.5B in total debt—extraordinary operating leverage on minimal balance-sheet risk. MSFT's Q2 revenue hit $81.3B (+16.7% YoY) with net income up 59.5% YoY to $38.5B, yielding a 47.3% net margin, which signals expanding profitability likely driven by cloud mix shift. On the other end, UNH's Q4 net income collapsed to essentially zero ($0.01B, -99.8% YoY) on $113.2B of revenue with $78.4B of debt—this is cash-flow compression I refuse to pay for until I see a credible margin recovery path. GOOGL also stands out positively with 18% revenue growth, 30.3% net margin, and a clean $14.8B debt load, while XOM's declining revenue (-1.3%) and shrinking earnings (-14.6%) on a 7.9% margin make it hard to get constructive.

views.note: 73% revenue growth, 63% net margin, and minimal debt of $8.5B represent best-in-class earnings power in the universe.
Net income surged 59.5% YoY to $38.5B on a 47.3% net margin with manageable $40.3B debt, reflecting durable cloud-driven profitability expansion.
18% revenue growth, 30.3% net margin, and low $14.8B debt make this a high-quality compounder; would reassess if ad revenue growth decelerates below 10%.
Revenue of $143.8B (+15.7% YoY) and 29.3% net margin are solid, though $88.5B in total debt and the need for continued services mix improvement temper my conviction.
Revenue grew 13.6% to $213.4B but net margin is only 9.9% and net income growth of 5.9% lags revenue growth, suggesting margin pressure from capex or AWS competition.
Revenue up 7.1% but net income declined 7% YoY; 28.4% margin is respectable for a bank but earnings trajectory is negative.
Only 1.5% revenue growth and a 6.7% net income decline signal limited pricing power; stable 19.4% margin keeps it from avoid territory.
Revenue jumped 18% but net income fell 13.9%, compressing margin to 12.5%—I need to see operating leverage materialize before getting constructive.
Revenue declined 1.3% with net income down 14.6% to $6.5B on a thin 7.9% margin; commodity cyclicality is working against earnings durability.
Net income collapsed 99.8% to essentially zero on $113.2B revenue with $78.4B debt—this is severe cash-flow compression and I need multiple quarters of margin recovery before reconsidering.

memos.headline: Fed on Pause at 3.75% as Rising Long Rates and Sticky Inflation Signal a Late-Cycle Squeeze
memos.body: I see the Fed firmly in pause mode: the upper bound has been flat at 3.75% for three months after 75 bps of cuts over the prior year, while headline CPI is running at 2.4% y/y—still above target and with a 0.7% three-month gain that annualizes uncomfortably high. The 10y yield has jumped 30 bps over the past quarter to 4.44%, and the 10y-2y spread has compressed 22 bps to just 0.46 pp, suggesting the market is repricing for higher-for-longer rates and possibly slower growth ahead. Unemployment at 4.4% is benign but has crept up 20 bps y/y, consistent with a mild softening rather than outright recession. My regime call is 'pause / late-cycle slowdown': duration-sensitive growth faces headwinds from the backup in long rates, banks benefit from a still-positive curve but the flattening trend is a caution, and defensives should outperform cyclicals. A CPI print above 2.6% y/y or unemployment breaking above 4.6% would force me to revisit this framework materially.

views.note: Duration-sensitive mega-cap faces headwinds from the 30 bps backup in the 10y, but pause regime limits further damage.
Similar duration exposure as AAPL; rising long rates cap multiple expansion, keeping me sidelined.
Highest-duration growth name in the universe is most vulnerable to the 10y at 4.44% and curve flattening.
Positive 10y-2y spread of 46 bps supports NIM, though the 22 bps quarterly compression tempers conviction.
Defensive staple should outperform in a late-cycle slowdown with unemployment drifting higher and the Fed on hold.
Cyclical bellwether faces headwinds from rising unemployment and higher long-end rates signaling slower growth.
Energy is idiosyncratic to oil prices; macro backdrop of mild slowdown is modestly negative but not decisive.
Defensive healthcare benefits from late-cycle positioning; sticky CPI supports pricing power in managed care.
Mixed exposure—consumer cyclical headwinds offset by cloud growth, but 10y backup limits re-rating.
Ad revenue tied to nominal GDP which is still growing, but higher discount rates keep me from getting constructive.

memos.headline: Post-Earnings Negative Reactions in AMZN and NVDA May Be Washed Out; UNH Leadership Churn Warrants Caution
memos.body: I am working with limited GDELT-style sentiment proxies today—primarily 8-K filings and their associated price reactions—so my conviction is tempered. AMZN dropped -5.6% on its Feb 5 earnings release and has since filed three additional 8-Ks including a material definitive agreement on Feb 27, suggesting the company is actively managing its narrative; the initial negative tone may be stabilizing. NVDA similarly fell -5.5% on its Feb 25 results, followed by a board-level change on Mar 6, which could signal either refreshment or instability—I lean toward the former given the sector's momentum but lack confirming tone data. UNH stands out negatively with two consecutive director/officer departure filings in late Feb and early Mar plus a Reg FD disclosure on Mar 9; that cadence of leadership turnover is unusual and likely generating negative media tone that may not yet be fully priced. XOM's muted +0.6% reaction to Jan 30 earnings and a subsequent officer change suggest a quiet, stable narrative—low noise, low risk.

views.note: The -5.6% earnings selloff is now seven weeks old and subsequent material agreement filing suggests narrative stabilization; tone likely turning up from a negative base.
The -5.5% post-earnings drop is a month old and board changes add uncertainty; waiting for clearer tone direction before taking a side.
Two officer/director departure filings in one week plus a Reg FD disclosure signal unusual leadership churn likely generating persistent negative media tone.
Quiet +0.6% earnings reaction and routine officer change suggest stable-to-positive tone with low noise—a favorable backdrop for energy exposure.
Minimal -0.5% earnings reaction and a board change in March leave tone flat; no clear directional signal.
A single 'Other Events' 8-K filed just yesterday provides no meaningful tone signal; staying on the sideline.

memos.headline: Surging Oil Prices and Policy Uncertainty Signal Escalating Geopolitical Stress Across the Portfolio
memos.body: I am seeing a confluence of geopolitical risk indicators that demands attention: WTI crude has spiked to $96.18/bbl (+70% over three months), the VIX has doubled to 27.44 over the same period, and the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index sits at an elevated 509.77 (+60% month-over-month). The oil move in particular looks structural rather than seasonal—a near-70% three-month surge implies either a major supply disruption (sanctions enforcement, conflict in a producing region) or a sharp escalation in energy-security concerns. High-yield spreads have widened modestly (+35bp over 3m to 3.21%) and the 10y-2y curve is flattening, consistent with markets pricing slower growth alongside a geopolitical risk premium. I have highest conviction on energy beneficiaries and lowest conviction on hardware names with deep China/Asia supply-chain exposure, where any new export controls or retaliatory tariffs would compound the demand hit from slowing growth. A de-escalation in whatever is driving the oil spike—or a rollback of trade restrictions—would change my view on the tech names.

views.note: XOM is the clearest beneficiary of the oil surge to $96 WTI; energy-security policy tailwinds reinforce the structural case.
Elevated policy uncertainty and the ongoing risk of tighter semiconductor export controls to China make NVDA the most exposed name in the universe.
Concentrated hardware supply chain in China leaves AAPL vulnerable to any escalation in tariffs or retaliatory measures amid surging policy uncertainty.
CAT benefits from infrastructure/energy capex but faces margin pressure from higher input costs and potential tariff headwinds; its fresh 8-K filing warrants monitoring.
Widening credit spreads and curve flattening are modest negatives, but JPM's diversified franchise and trading revenues can absorb geopolitical vol; staying neutral until spreads widen further.
Higher energy costs pressure logistics margins, but AMZN's cloud business is less directly exposed to trade-policy risk; multiple recent 8-Ks suggest active corporate developments worth tracking.
Less hardware supply-chain exposure than AAPL/NVDA but regulatory and antitrust policy risk remains a structural overhang.

plan.summary: The portfolio leans into the oil surge via XOM and the cleanest technical setup in CAT, while keeping a quality-growth barbell through GOOGL (deeply oversold with strong fundamentals) and a modest NVDA position sized down due to geopolitical headwinds. Heavy cash (~40%) reflects elevated VIX, policy uncertainty, and a late-cycle macro regime where capital preservation matters.
